questions.problem: Let $I=[0,2]⊂R$ and ${X}_{i}=\{i\}\times [0,i].$ Which of the following represents ${⋂}_{i\in I}{X}_{i}?$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that the intersection of a family of indexed sets consists of those elements that belong to *all* the sets:

$$
{⋂}_{i\in I}{A}_{i}=\{x\,:\,x\in {A}_{k}\,\,\text{for all}\,\,k\in I\}
$$

Let's now write down one of our indexed sets. For example, if $i=1,$ we have 

$$
{X}_{1}=\{1\}\times [0,1]=\{(1,k)\,:\,k\in [0,1]\}.
$$

This represents a vertical line segment from the point $(1,0)$ to the point $(1,1)$ in the coordinate plane, as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14249122/assets/71dd97607df48caf579c2e476520507ede035f65c336064f022cd900b6c120fc.png)

In general,

$$
{X}_{i}=\{i\}\times [0,i]=\{(i,k)\,:\,k\in [0,i]\}
$$

is the vertical line segment from the point $(i,0)$ to the point $(i,i).$ 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14249122/assets/4b87c830620f54e5b3a3bb7923be971b4d9d4abb98cfb3dcdc8387f376a0b452.png)

There are no points that lie in all sets. Therefore, the intersection of the indexed sets is $∅,$ the empty set.

questions.problem: Which of the following is a representation of the set $S={R}^{+}\times Z$ in the Cartesian plane?
questions.worked_solution:
The Cartesian product $A\times B$ consists of all ordered pairs whose first coordinate belongs to $A$ and whose second coordinate belongs to $B.$

$$
A\times B=\{(a,b)\,:\,a\in A,\,b\in B\}
$$

In this case, the set 

$$
S={R}^{+}\times Z
$$

 
contains every point in ${R}^{2}$ whose $x$-coordinate is a positive real number and whose $y$-coordinate is an integer number.

$$
S=\{(x,y)\,:\,x\in {R}^{+},\,y\in Z\}
$$

To visualize $S,$ consider ${S}_{-1}⊂S$ containing all points whose $x$-coordinate is any positive real number and whose $y$-coordinate equals $-1.$

$$
{S}_{-1}=\{(x,-1)\,:\,x\in {R}^{+}\}
$$

We can represent ${S}_{-1}$ in the plane as follows:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14249122/assets/50228bcff5b3678518379cda03257ac234e8312cd23f9b38fa897188c8c5c1c5.png)

Next, consider ${S}_{1}⊂S$ containing all points whose $x$-coordinate is any positive real number and whose $y$-coordinate equals $1.$

$$
{S}_{1}=\{(x,1)\,:\,x\in {R}^{+}\}.
$$

We can represent ${S}_{1}$ in the plane as follows:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14249122/assets/75f8be8dd49241503b705c78e4018a98fead197191b38f856d7fbce069a63de2.png)

We can create the subsets $…,{S}_{-3},{S}_{-2},{S}_{0},{S}_{2},{S}_{3},…$ similarly. Our Cartesian product consists of the *union* of these subsets:

$$
\begin{aligned}{R}^{+}\times Z & =…{S}_{-2}\cup {S}_{-1}\cup {S}_{0}\cup {S}_{1}\cup {S}_{2}\cup {S}_{3}\cup … \\  & ={⋃}_{i\in Z}{S}_{i}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can visualize ${R}^{+}\times Z$ as the set of horizontal lines shown in the diagram below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14249122/assets/2086bcf65608ff2c031da9f6882272fd6d8eb828f3d904c4f0fc946b5fbe108c.png)

questions.problem: Which of the following is a representation of the set $S=[0,2]\times \{-1,0,1\}$ in the Cartesian plane?
questions.worked_solution:
The Cartesian product $A\times B$ consists of all ordered pairs whose first coordinate belongs to $A$ and whose second coordinate belongs to $B.$

$$
A\times B=\{(a,b)\,:\,a\in A,\,b\in B\}
$$

In this case, the set 

$$
S=[0,2]\times \{-1,0,1\}
$$

contains every point in ${R}^{2}$ whose $x$-coordinate is any real number in the interval $[0,2]$ and whose $y$-coordinate is either $-1,0,$ or $1.$

$$
S=\{(x,y)\,:\,x\in [0,2],\,y\in \{-1,0,1\}\}.
$$

To visualize $S$, consider ${S}_{1}⊂S$ containing all points whose $x$-coordinate is any real number in the interval $[0,2]$ and whose $y$-coordinate equals $-1$

$$
{S}_{1}=\{(x,-1)\,:\,x\in [0,2]\}
$$

This set is represented by the line segment shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14249122/assets/de9bd6dc79cabf8230b0cec26233958aa0fbb001875b9942cbb7f4d36e6b08fb.png)

Next, consider ${S}_{2}⊂S$ containing all points whose $x$-coordinate is any real number in the interval $[0,2]$ and whose $y$-coordinate equals $0.$

$$
{S}_{2}=\{(x,0)\,:\,x\in [0,2]\}.
$$

This set is represented by the line segment shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14249122/assets/819c31e4d29dbd3e18c7dea8df495a565d2ede866ec019c764704d6dc47f5c70.png)

Now, consider ${S}_{3}⊂S$ containing all points whose $x$-coordinate is any real number in the interval $[0,2]$ and whose $y$-coordinate equals $1.$

$$
{S}_{3}=\{(x,1)\,:\,x\in [0,2]\}.
$$

This set is represented by the line segment shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14249122/assets/3f335df98dc9cb33ccc96f87d24efa3bd78a4d4c271d0fbaf7ae5e8c30916d9e.png)

Our Cartesian product is the *union* of these subsets:

$$
S={S}_{1}\cup {S}_{2}\cup {S}_{3}
$$

Therefore, $S$ can be represented by the three line segments shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14249122/assets/a1a9065f9dbb6648100bc6a22bff367916c241dc2eba5f3878d6cf1b9821d4e8.png)

$$
{⋃}_{i\in I}{A}_{i}=\{x\,:\,x\in {A}_{k}\,\,\text{for at least one}\,\,k\in I\}

Let's now write down one of our indexed sets. For example, if $i=0.5,$ we have 

$$
{X}_{0.5}=[0.5,1]\times \{0.5\}=\{(k,0.5)\,:\,k\in [0.5,1]\}.

$$
{X}_{i}=[i,1]\times \{i\}=\{(k,i)\,:\,k\in [i,1]\}

is the horizontal line segment from the point $(i,i)$ to the point $(1,i).$ 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14249122/assets/f255d7dede080e93cb135c1087a0f14591467439d891187062a4fa185a8858cf.png)
